author: cerebral_barrier
text_post: These days, (when I have time) I read mostly Popular Science, Popular Mechanics, gun magazines, National geographic and anything involving space travel or military hardware, although I tend to snatch up anything that catches my interest.    I used to actually buy books about the topics I liked, but moving out on my own requires me to be more thrifty with my hobbies.   Whenever I see books being given away by libraries or schools, I'll often snag a few.   My most recent finds were Jane's Warships of WWI and WWII. When I was growing up, I used to have an old medical science book about 2 inches thick.   I read that thing cover to cover like a comic book.  The knowledge is now part of my baseline for self treatment.  All I need to do is go recertify myself for CPR, buy more advanced medical gear and then I'm all set.   Nowadays, my time is kind of limited, due to my new job and the associated commute but I do a lot of work in medical establishments so I tend to "borrow" their magazines and medical brochures when I get the chance.   I'm also a huge fan of anything involving alternative energy production (eg; solar, wind, gasification, thermal siphoning etc.)    I also read articles on the internet about these subjects as well, but tend to do so with skepticism due to conflicting information.   It's up to the reader to do their own research and determine which position is most likely to be true.  After all, it is impossible to truly "know" something without experiencing it and/or witnessing it first hand.  I'm one of those weirdos who just has to know how and why things work.   It doesn't really matter what the subject is; I need to know how and why it exists and how and why it works or doesn't work.   If written information isn't available, I'll make personal observations and take notes of any recurring patterns I see.   When I buy my next house I plan to put what I've learned to use by building a three option power grid, consisting of solar power as the primary source, public utilities as a backup and a wood-gas system to burn leaves, wood debris and waste paper (I get a lot of junkmail) to heat water through thermo-siphoning and simultaneously create fuel for an emergency generator.  If I can safely store the gas, I may even be able to make modifications to my cars so they can operate on the gas in the event of another oil crisis.   For heat, I've built a small prototype solar air heater.   It works but is too small to be useful.  However, the design can be upscaled, placed outside and used to heat both water and air before delivering them indoors. Human psychology in particular is of great interest to me as well since it governs our lives with regard to how we coexist with others.    There is a lot of written information available on the subject, as well as several billion humans to "experiment" on ...as you've just witnessed.   With enough practice, you can learn to influence or even control how an interaction proceeds.   The psychology behind DSR allows for this as well but has a much greater emphasis on materialism, aesthetics and artificial social protocols.    Thank you for turning this thread back into something more positive.  We really need more of this around here.   What kinds of things do you like to read about?
